meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, this line is Virginia Woolf's — from A Room of One's Own (1929). We trace it to the primary text and flag a famous 2014 misquotation of it.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This exact sentence appears in A Room of One’s Own (1929), Chapter 1, in the passage describing the plain college dinner of “beef and prunes” that followed the lavish men’s-college lunch.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 28 September 1929 (Hogarth Press, London; Harcourt, Brace & Co., New York)

source.excerpt: The human frame being what it is, heart, body and brain all mixed together, and not contained in separate compartments as they will be no doubt in another million years, a good dinner is of great importance to good talk. One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well. The lamp in the spine does not light on beef and prunes.
trail: First delivered as lectures at Newnham College and Girton College, Cambridge, in October 1928, then expanded and published as A Room of One’s Own in 1929 (see Wikipedia overview ↗).
The exact sentence is preserved in the full text of Chapter 1 as hosted on Wikisource ↗ and independently on Project Gutenberg Australia ↗.
The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ confirms “think well” (not “eat well”) is the correct wording, citing a 2014 Marks & Spencer bag that garbled the line.
source.excerptNote: From the narrator’s reflection after a meagre dinner at the fictional women’s college of Fernham, contrasted earlier in the chapter with an opulent lunch at a men’s college.

author.name: Virginia Woolf
author.heading: About Virginia Woolf
author.bio: Virginia Woolf was a leading figure of English literary modernism, known for novels including Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse. A Room of One’s Own (1929), drawn from lectures she gave at two Cambridge women’s colleges, is her landmark essay on women, money, and creative independence.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The quote is genuinely Woolf’s, but a widely circulated commercial version of it swapped one word and broke the sentence’s logic.

items.why: M&S printed the line as “One cannot eat well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well,” which is internally contradictory since “eat” and “dined” can’t both stand, as documented by the Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Woolf’s original word is “think,” not “eat” — confirmed against the 1929 text of A Room of One’s Own, Chapter 1 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line sits at the close of the essay’s opening chapter, immediately after Woolf’s narrator compares two Cambridge college meals: a sumptuous lunch of sole, partridge, and wine at a men’s college, followed by a plain dinner of “beef and prunes” at the women’s college of Fernham.

Woolf uses the contrast to make a material argument: that women’s intellectual and creative disadvantage was not just about talent or opportunity but about literal resources — food, income, and space — that men’s institutions had and women’s did not.
